questions.q: Where does the Calculated Field option live in the PivotTable ribbon?
options: Analyze tab → Calculations group → Fields, Items, & Sets
Insert tab → Charts group
Home tab → Number Format group
Design tab → PivotTable Styles group
questions.explain: With a cell inside the PivotTable selected, the Analyze tab's Calculations group has a Fields, Items, & Sets menu, which is where Calculated Field opens its Name/Formula dialog.

questions.q: In a calculated field formula like `=Profit/Revenue`, what values does it actually operate on?
options: The aggregated (summed) totals of Profit and Revenue for each row/column combination, not row-by-row values
A single hard-coded pair of numbers typed into the dialog
The raw, unaggregated values from the very first row of source data only
Values from a completely different, unrelated PivotTable
questions.explain: A calculated field's formula references other fields already in the PivotTable by name and computes using their aggregated totals — a ratio of sums, not an average of individual row ratios.

questions.q: What does 'Show Values As' (via Value Field Settings) let you do without writing a formula?
options: Display a field using a built-in computed view like % of Grand Total or Running Total
Rename the PivotTable entirely
Convert the PivotTable into a PivotChart
Delete a field from the source Table
questions.explain: Show Values As offers built-in custom calculations — percentages of totals, running totals, and more — reached from the same Values-field context menu, with no formula required.

questions.q: Why can't a calculated column of per-row percentages correctly represent a blended percentage at a subtotal level?
options: Summing or averaging already-computed per-row percentages doesn't equal the true ratio of the summed numerator to the summed denominator
Calculated columns are not allowed to contain percentages at all
Excel automatically blocks percentage columns from being subtotaled
There is no actual difference — both approaches always produce identical subtotal results
questions.explain: A calculated field computes the ratio using the totals aggregated at each level of the PivotTable, which is mathematically correct — averaging or summing individual row percentages is not equivalent to that ratio-of-sums.

questions.q: According to the lesson's rule of thumb, when should you use a calculated column on the source data instead of a PivotTable calculated field?
options: When other parts of the workbook (other formulas, charts, or PivotTables) need the per-row value directly
Whenever a PivotTable exists at all, calculated columns should always be preferred
Only when the source data has fewer than 10 rows
Calculated columns should never be used under any circumstance
questions.explain: A calculated column makes the per-row value visible and usable everywhere in the workbook, not just inside one PivotTable — which is exactly when it's the better choice over a calculated field.
